title: Quantum simulation of the Heisenberg XXZ model on a Rydberg atom array
abstract: A major application of analog quantum hardware is quantum simulation, where a system evolves over time according to a given Hamiltonian. One challenge when implementing the Hamiltonian on a programmable quantum simulator is the availability of distinct coupling types, many of which go beyond the conventional ZZ-couplings found in Ising Hamiltonians that are naturally implemented by various platforms. In prior work, we have developed a method based on domain wall encoding to simulate one-dimensional spin chains using only Ising Hamiltonians, which would otherwise require XX+YY-couplings as well. Here, we implement the method on a commercially accessible Rydberg atom quantum device, and simulate the time evolution of the Heisenberg XXZ model with various anisotropies. We successfully probe the XY and Ising phases of the model and reproduce the qualitative behavior of several one- and two-body observables in both phases, as well as at the critical point. Our work augments the toolbox to simulate canonical quantum many-body systems on analog quantum simulators.
summary: This paper details the quantum simulation of the Heisenberg XXZ model using Rydberg atom arrays. The core innovation is using domain wall encoding to simulate the full XXZ model by mapping it onto an effective Ising Hamiltonian realizable on the hardware. The authors successfully validate this method by reproducing expected physical behavior across different quantum phases while rigorously accounting for realistic experimental noise sources.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating the Heisenberg XXZ model on quantum hardware by implementing a method that allows for the simulation of necessary coupling types beyond conventional ZZ-couplings.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrate the implementation of this simulation method on a Rydberg atom quantum device, reproducing the expected dynamical behavior across XY, Ising, and critical phases of the model.
method: The simulation employs domain wall encoding to map the target XXZ spin chain Hamiltonian onto an effective Ising Hamiltonian, which is then realized using the native interactions of the Rydberg atom array.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a Rydberg atom array (e.g., QuEra's Aquila device) used as an analog quantum simulator. The target model is the Heisenberg XXZ chain, and the simulation relies on mapping its dynamics onto an effective Ising model via domain wall encoding.
key_observables: Site populations ($p_i$), normalized correlations ($\Gamma_{ij}/\max_{ij} \Gamma_{ij}$), and fidelity (state and classical).
important_parameters: Anisotropy ($\delta$) is probed across XY ($\delta=0.0$), isotropic ($\delta=1.0$), and Ising ($\delta=4.0$) regimes. Error sources include thermal motion, laser fluctuations, and readout errors.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that undesired interactions beyond next-nearest-neighbor are negligible, and the error model incorporates specific approximations for disorder and readout errors.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the zig-zag atom arrangement realizing required interactions, the mapping process from XXZ to Ising via domain wall encoding, and comparisons of fidelity and correlation functions across different error models and anisotropies.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the theoretical framework by first defining the required Hamiltonian, then detailing the domain wall encoding transformation, and finally implementing and analyzing the simulation results using a comprehensive error model that includes disorder and readout errors.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of quantum simulation by demonstrating how to engineer complex Hamiltonians (like XXZ) on platforms (Rydberg atoms) whose native interactions might otherwise be limited, thereby expanding the accessible model space for quantum many-body physics.
